questions.question: What is the difference between for, while, and do-while loops in Java?
questions.title: for vs while vs do-while Loops in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`for`** loops fit when you know the iteration count in advance. **`while`** loops run as long as a condition is true, checked **before** each iteration (may run zero times). **`do-while`** loops check the condition **after** the body, so they always execute at least once.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when to select each loop construct based on iteration requirements and condition placement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing that do-while guarantees at least one execution, leading to the wrong loop choice in validation scenarios
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Provide concrete real-world scenarios: for with collections, while with stream reading, do-while with menu systems that must display once

sections.title: All Three Loops Repeat Code — the Real Difference Is When the Condition Is Checked
sections.content:
A loop is a way to repeat the same block of code without writing it out by hand many times. If you wanted to print the numbers 1 to 100, you would not type a hundred separate print statements — you write one and tell Java to repeat it. That single idea is exactly what `for`, `while`, and `do-while` all do.

So why does Java ship three different loops if they all just repeat code? Because they differ in **when the condition is checked** and **how much of the counting work the loop manages for you**. Picking the wrong one usually still runs — but the right one makes your intent obvious and quietly removes whole categories of bugs.

Here is how each one works. The **`for` loop** is the counted loop: it packs three things into one line — where to start, when to stop, and how to step forward. `for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)` means start at zero, stop before ten, add one each time, so you know the exact number of runs before the loop even begins. The **`while` loop** is the conditional loop: it has no built-in counter and simply keeps going while a condition stays true, which fits when you do not know the count ahead of time — reading a file until it ends, or draining a queue until it is empty. Both `for` and `while` check the condition **before** the body, so if it starts false, the body never runs even once.

In an interview, the loop that actually earns marks is the third one. The **`do-while` loop** checks its condition **after** the body instead of before, so it always runs at least one time — that is its entire reason to exist. Here is the gotcha freshers trip on: a `do-while` executes once even when the condition was false from the very start. That is perfect for a menu or login prompt that has to show before it can ask the user whether to continue, but it is a nasty surprise if you assumed it behaves like `while`. A quick rule to carry in: reach for `for` when you have a count, `while` when you are waiting for something to change, and `do-while` when the first run must always happen.

sections.title: How Each Loop's Condition Check Differs
sections.content:
The key structural difference between all three loops is where the condition lives. Here is that difference visualized — notice how `for` and `while` both check before entering the body, while `do-while` checks after. ```mermaid flowchart TD A(["Start"]) --> B{"for / while:
Check condition"} B -- "false" --> C(["Skip loop entirely"]) B -- "true" --> D["Run body"] D --> E["Update (for only)"] E --> B F(["Start"]) --> G["do-while:
Run body FIRST"] G --> H{"Check condition"} H -- "true" --> G H -- "false" --> I(["Exit loop"]) ``` `for` and `while` share the same structure — condition checked first, body may never run. `do-while` flips the order — body always runs at least once, condition checked afterward.

blue|while|~Conditional entry|checks before body|zero iterations possible|read until EOF
emerald|do-while|~Guaranteed first run|checks after body|at least one iteration|menus, validation
rose|Watch out|~Make progress|update the control var|else infinite loop|arrays are zero-indexed

sections.title: Loop Type Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | for | while | do-while |
|---|---|---|---|
| Condition check | Before each iteration | Before each iteration | After each iteration |
| Minimum executions | Zero if condition false | Zero if condition false | Always at least one |
| Best for | Known iteration count | Unknown iteration count | Menus, validation prompts |
| Typical use | Array traversal | Reading until EOF | Input validation loops |

sections.title: The Off-By-One That Crashes Every Fresher's First Loop
sections.content:
The most common loop bug isn't faulty logic — it's the boundary condition. The trap is reaching for `<=` when the array length means you actually want `<`.

```java
int[] a = {10, 20, 30};
for (int i = 0; i <= a.length; i++) { // i reaches 3 → out of bounds
    System.out.println(a[i]);         // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
}
```
The array holds three elements at indices 0, 1, and 2, but `a.length` is 3. With `<=`, `i` climbs all the way to 3 and `a[3]` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime — it compiles fine and only blows up when that line executes.

sections.title: Why < Is the Right Boundary for length
Each Loop Matched to the Job It Was Built For
When to Use Each Loop
sections.content:
Use **`for` loops** when iterating over a collection of known size, processing array indices, or repeating a specific number of times — validating 10 inputs or processing 100 records.

Use **`while` loops** when termination isn't based on a counter but on external state — reading until a sentinel value, processing a queue until empty, retrying until success.

Use **`do-while` loops** when the body must run at least once before checking — displaying a menu, prompting for input with validation, or a game loop that renders the first frame before checking for quit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `while` where `do-while` fits** — you duplicate the body once above the loop to force a first run, and the two copies drift apart over time into a maintenance bug.
- **`i <= array.length` instead of `i < array.length`** — the loop reaches an index that doesn't exist and throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at runtime, after compiling cleanly.
- **Forgetting to advance the control variable** — a `while` whose condition never flips to false spins forever, pinning a CPU core and hanging the thread.
- **Dropping the semicolon after `do { } while (cond)`** — it's a compile error unique to `do-while`, and freshers who only ever wrote `for`/`while` miss it on their first try.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **for** — best when the iteration count is known; commonly used with indices.
- **while** — condition checked before the first run; may never execute.
- **do-while** — condition checked after; guarantees at least one iteration.
- **Infinite loops** — happen when the condition never becomes false; ensure progress.
- **break/continue** — work in all three loop types.
- **Zero-indexed** — for an array of n elements, valid indices are 0 to n-1.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
When I pick a loop, the first question I ask is **whether I know the count or I'm waiting on something**. If I know it — fifty records, the length of an array, a fixed range — I reach for a `for` loop, because the start, the stop, and the step all sit in one header where the iteration count is obvious at a glance. If I don't know the count and I'm waiting for the world to change — a file to hit end of input, a queue to drain, a user to type quit — that's a `while` loop, and because it **checks the condition before the first pass**, it can legitimately **run zero times**.

The `do-while` is the one people misuse. It **checks the condition after the body**, so it **always runs at least once**, which is exactly what a menu or a login prompt needs — you have to show something before you can read a response. The tell that someone reached for the wrong loop is **duplicated display code sitting above a `while` loop**. If you're copying the body just to force a first run, it should have been a `do-while`.

questions.question: What is the difference between break, continue, and return in Java?
questions.title: break vs continue vs return in Java Loops
questions.direct_answer: **`break`** exits the loop entirely and resumes after it. **`continue`** skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one. **`return`** exits the entire method immediately — terminating not just the loop but the method itself.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise understanding of control flow statements that affect loop and method execution differently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing break with return, thinking break exits the method or that continue exits the loop entirely
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention labeled break and continue for nested loops, and demonstrate understanding of early return patterns for cleaner code

sections.title: break Stops the Loop, return Stops the Method — That One Gap Is the Whole Trap
sections.content:
Normally a loop runs every line in its body, checks the condition, and goes around again. `break`, `continue`, and `return` are three keywords that let you interrupt that normal flow on purpose. The reason there are three of them is that each one interrupts at a different level.

Why would you want to stop early? Because often you simply do not need the rest. Once you have found the record you were searching for, scanning the remaining thousand items is wasted work. Once an item turns out to be invalid, you want to skip it and move on. These keywords give you that control instead of forcing every iteration to run to completion.

The simplest way to keep them straight is to picture zoom levels. **`continue`** is the smallest: it abandons just the current iteration — skip the rest of this one pass and jump to the next round — while the loop itself keeps running. **`break`** zooms out one level and exits the whole loop immediately; execution lands on the first line after the loop. **`return`** is the biggest of the three: it exits the **entire method**, no matter how many loops or if-blocks you are nested inside, and it can hand a value back to whoever called the method.

In real code, the most elegant use is the **early-return pattern**. Instead of wrapping your logic in deeper and deeper if-else blocks, you check a precondition at the top of the method and `return` immediately if it fails, which leaves the main path flat and easy to read.

Two gotchas catch freshers. First, `break` stops the loop but the method keeps running — so any code after the loop still executes; if you wanted the method itself to end, you needed `return`, not `break`. Second, a plain `break` only escapes the **innermost** loop. To jump out of several nested loops at once, Java offers a **labeled `break`**: put a label before the outer loop and write `break labelName` to leave both at once. The same labeling trick works with `continue`.

sections.title: Where Each Statement Sends Execution
sections.content:
Here is the control flow for all three statements. Notice how `continue` stays inside the loop, `break` exits the loop but stays in the method, and `return` exits the method entirely.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A(["Loop iteration starts"]) --> B{"Check condition"}
    B -- "false" --> Z(["After loop — method continues"])
    B -- "true" --> C["Run body"]
    C --> D{"Hit a keyword?"}
    D -- "continue" --> E["Skip rest of body"]
    E --> B
    D -- "break" --> Z
    D -- "return" --> R(["Exit method entirely → back to caller"])
    D -- "neither" --> F["Finish body normally"]
    F --> B
```

`continue` loops back to the condition check. `break` jumps past the loop. `return` leaves the method — the loop and everything else in the method is abandoned.

sections.title: break vs continue vs return at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|continue|~Skip this iteration|jumps to next loop pass|loop keeps running|skip invalid items
blue|break|~Exit this loop|resumes after the loop|innermost only|stop once found
emerald|return|~Exit the method|leaves all loops|sends back a value|early-exit pattern
rose|Labeled break|~Exit outer loops|outer: for(...)|break outer;|for deep nesting

sections.title: Control Flow Statement Comparison
sections.content:
| Statement | Scope of effect | What happens next | Common use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `break` | Exits innermost loop/switch | Continues after the loop | Found target, stop searching |
| `continue` | Skips rest of iteration | Jumps to next iteration | Skip invalid items |
| `return` | Exits entire method | Returns to caller immediately | Early exit with a result |

sections.title: The Nested-Loop Bug: break Only Escapes One Level
How a Labeled break Escapes Every Level at Once
Seeing All Three Side by Side: The Scope Each One Affects
When to Use Each Statement
sections.content:
Use **`break`** when you've found what you want and there's no point continuing — searching for a user and stopping once found.

Use **`continue`** to skip certain items but keep iterating — filtering invalid records, skipping nulls.

Use **`return`** when your method's result is ready — the early-return pattern is great for validation: check preconditions at the top and `return` early, avoiding deep nesting. For nested loops, labeled `break`/`continue` affect outer loops.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Writing `break` where you meant `return`** — the loop ends but the rest of the method keeps running, so cleanup or summary code executes when you expected the method to be finished, producing wrong results.
- **Using `continue` when you needed `break`** — you skip the current item but keep scanning the entire rest of the collection, turning an O(1) early exit into an O(n) waste on large inputs.
- **Assuming `break` escapes nested loops** — a plain `break` only leaves the innermost loop, so the outer loop silently re-enters and repeats work that has side effects; use a labeled `break outer` instead.
- **Putting unreachable code after `return` in a loop** — `return` inside the loop can make a trailing statement unreachable, which is a compile error, not a warning.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **break** — terminates the innermost loop or switch; execution resumes after it.
- **continue** — skips the rest of the current iteration; proceeds to the next.
- **return** — exits the entire method, bypassing all enclosing loops.
- **Labeled break/continue** — `outer: for(...)` lets you affect outer loops.
- **Early return** — returning early from validation avoids deep nesting.
- **Scope** — `break` affects loop scope; `return` affects method scope.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The fastest way I keep these straight is to think about **what each one walks away from**. `continue` walks away from the current iteration only — it skips the rest of this pass and the loop keeps going, which is perfect for filtering, like skipping invalid orders while still processing the rest. `break` walks away from the whole loop — once I've found the record I was searching for, there's no point scanning further, so I `break` and execution picks up on the line right after the loop. `return` walks away from the **entire method**, no matter how deep I'm nested; three loops and an if-block down, `return` still hands control straight back to the caller, optionally with a value.

The distinction that actually matters is **`break` versus `return`**, because that's where the bugs hide. `break` ends the loop but the method keeps running, so any code after the loop still executes — if you wanted the method itself to be done, you needed `return`. Two things I'd add to show real experience: the **early-return pattern**, where you validate preconditions at the top and `return` immediately instead of nesting if-else, and **labeled `break`** for nested loops, since a plain `break` only exits the innermost one. My default is to lean on `return` for clean early exits — it almost always reads better than threading a flag variable through the loop.

questions.question: What is the enhanced for-each loop in Java and when should you use it?
questions.title: Enhanced for-each Loop in Java
questions.direct_answer: The **enhanced for-each loop** (Java 5) iterates over arrays and any `Iterable` collection **without an index counter**. It's cleaner and less error-prone than a traditional `for` loop when you only need to read elements and don't need the index.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate writes idiomatic modern Java versus using C-style for loops for everything
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using for-each when you need the index, or trying to modify the array through the loop variable, which doesn't work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that for-each calls iterator() behind the scenes for collections, and that you can't remove elements during iteration without Iterator.remove or removeIf

sections.title: Why For-Each Exists: It Deletes the Five Moving Parts of an Index Loop
sections.content:
The **`for-each`** loop is a shorter, cleaner way to go through every element in an array or collection. You name a variable for the element and the thing you want to walk through, and Java visits each item for you — that is the whole feature.

Why does it exist? Because the older way was fiddly. To loop a list with a traditional `for`, you write five separate things: create an index `i`, start it at zero, check it against the size, read the element at `i`, and increment `i`. Four of those five are **pure bookkeeping** that has nothing to do with your real goal — and that bookkeeping is exactly where off-by-one bugs are born. `for-each` removes all of it.

The syntax is `for (Type variable : collection)`, where the colon reads as "in." So `for (String name : names)` is simply "for each String name in names." Under the hood it is **not magic**: for **arrays** the compiler generates ordinary index access, and for **collections** — anything that implements `Iterable` — it calls `iterator()` and loops with `hasNext()` and `next()`. That is why `for-each` works on `List`, `Set`, `Queue`, and any custom class that implements `Iterable`.

It arrived in Java 5 and quickly became the idiomatic style. Reaching for a C-style index loop just to read values now signals unfamiliarity with modern Java, which interviewers notice. The catch worth knowing is that `for-each` gives you a **read view**: the loop variable is a copy of the reference (or the value, for primitives), so reassigning it — `name = "new"` — changes only the local variable, never the element in the collection.

That read-view nature is also where the classic gotcha lives. You cannot add or remove elements from the collection during a `for-each` loop — the iterator detects the structural change underneath it and throws a `ConcurrentModificationException` at runtime. For those operations, reach for `removeIf()`, an explicit `Iterator` with `iterator.remove()`, or a separate list to collect changes. And when you genuinely need the index — to print "item 1 of 10" or to write new values into an array — that is your signal to go back to a traditional `for` loop. `for-each` is purely a **read-all-elements construct**.

sections.title: For-Each vs Traditional For — What the Compiler Does
sections.content:
Both loops ultimately do the same traversal, but for-each hides the plumbing. Here is what each one really does at execution time.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph FOR_EACH ["for-each (collection)"]
        direction TB
        A1["Call iterator()"] --> B1{"hasNext()"}
        B1 -- "yes" --> C1["element = next()"]
        C1 --> D1["Run body"]
        D1 --> B1
        B1 -- "no" --> E1(["Done"])
    end

    subgraph TRAD_FOR ["traditional for (array)"]
        direction TB
        A2["int i = 0"] --> B2{"i < length"}
        B2 -- "true" --> C2["element = arr[i]"]
        C2 --> D2["Run body"]
        D2 --> E2["i++"]
        E2 --> B2
        B2 -- "false" --> F2(["Done"])
    end
```

For-each on collections uses the `Iterator` pattern internally. For arrays, it uses index access. The for-each syntax is a clean abstraction over both.

sections.title: for-each at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Syntax|~for (T x : coll)|no index counter|no bounds checking|Java 5+
blue|Works on|~Arrays + Iterable|List, Set, Queue|calls iterator()|arrays use index internally
emerald|Read-only intent|~Variable is a copy|reassign does nothing|no current index|use plain for if you need i
rose|Pitfall|~No structural edits|remove throws CME|use removeIf|or Iterator.remove()

sections.title: The CME Trap: Removing While You Iterate
The Fix: Let removeIf Drive the Iterator for You
sections.content:
The clean fix is to hand the whole filter to the collection so it manages the iterator internally.

```java
List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "bad", "c"));
items.removeIf(s -> s.equals("bad")); // [a, c]
```
For structural changes during traversal, reach for `removeIf` or an explicit `Iterator` with `iterator.remove()` — both mutate the list through the same iterator that's tracking it, so the modification counter stays consistent and there's no exception.

sections.title: When For-Each Wins — and the One Case Where You Drop Back to an Index
When to Use For-Each
sections.content:
Use **`for-each`** when iterating over every element and only reading values — summing, filtering, printing. It's perfect for processing a list of orders or validating each input.

**Don't use `for-each`** in these cases:
- When you need the **index**.
- When you need to modify the collection during iteration (`ConcurrentModificationException`).
- When iterating with a custom step.
- When iterating backward.

In those cases use a traditional `for` loop or `IntStream.range`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding or removing during iteration** — calling `list.remove(x)` inside a for-each throws `ConcurrentModificationException` at runtime and aborts your loop mid-pass; use `removeIf()` or an explicit `Iterator.remove()` instead.
- **Expecting the loop variable to write back** — `for (String s : list) { s = "new"; }` silently does nothing, because `s` is a copy of the reference; you change the local, the list keeps its old values, and you ship a no-op.
- **Reaching for for-each when you need the index** — bolting on a manual counter to print "item 3 of 10" reintroduces exactly the off-by-one risk for-each removed; use a traditional `for` when position matters.
- **For-each over a possibly-null collection** — `for (var x : maybeNull)` throws `NullPointerException`, since for-each calls `iterator()` on the reference; guard nulls before the loop.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Syntax** — `for (Type x : collection)` removes index management.
- **Works with** — arrays and any `Iterable` (`List`, `Set`, `Queue`).
- **Under the hood** — indices for arrays; `iterator()` for collections.
- **Read-only intent** — the loop variable is a copy; reassigning it changes nothing.
- **No index** — if you need the position, use a traditional `for`.
- **CME** — adding/removing during iteration throws `ConcurrentModificationException`; use `removeIf`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
`for-each` is my default for reading a collection, and the reason is concrete: it **deletes the index bookkeeping where almost every off-by-one bug lives**. I just say for each order in orders and do the work — no counter, no length check, nothing to get wrong at the boundary. Under the hood it **isn't magic**. For collections the compiler turns it into an `Iterator`, calling `hasNext` and `next`; for arrays it's plain index access.

That detail explains the classic trap. If you remove from a list while a `for-each` is walking it, the iterator sees the structure change underneath it and throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. So when I actually need to delete during traversal, I use `removeIf` or an explicit `Iterator`'s remove method. The only two times I drop back to a traditional `for` loop are when I need the **index position**, or when I'm **writing values back into an array** — `for-each` hands you a copy of each element, not a slot you can assign to. For everything else, which is most of the time, `for-each` is the **cleaner, safer choice**.

questions.question: What will the following code output and why? A switch case with a missing break statement.
questions.title: Switch Fall-Through Gotcha in Java
questions.direct_answer: Without **`break`**, a `switch` **falls through** to the next case and executes it too, regardless of whether it matched. Execution runs from the first matching case downward until a `break` or the end of the switch — a classic Java gotcha.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to detail and understanding of switch fall-through semantics — interviewers frequently test this with code-reading questions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming each case executes independently like if-else branches, not realizing missing break causes sequential execution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that fall-through is sometimes intentional for grouping cases, and that Java 14+ arrow switch syntax eliminates the issue entirely

sections.title: Why a switch With One Missing break Runs Code You Never Matched
sections.content:
A `switch` statement chooses which block of code to run based on the value of a single variable. You hand it a value, list several `case` labels, and it jumps to the one that matches — a tidy alternative to a long chain of if-else checks.

Why do you even need the `break` keyword inside it? Because of a twist that trips up almost every beginner, and it is the whole point of this question. When a case matches, classic Java switch does **not** run just that one case and stop. It jumps to the matching case and then keeps executing — the next case, and the one after that — until it hits a `break` statement or reaches the end of the switch. This behavior is called **fall-through**, and Java inherited it from the C language.

Picture a `switch` on the number 2 with cases for 1, 2, 3, and a `default`. If `case` 2 has no `break`, Java runs the case-2 code, then falls straight into `case` 3 and runs it, then into `default` and runs that too. Three blocks execute even though only one value matched. The `break` keyword is the explicit stop sign: it tells the `switch` "done here, jump past the end." Without it, execution pours downward regardless of whether the next label actually matches.

Why keep such a sharp edge in the language? Because fall-through is occasionally useful on purpose — stacking labels with no code between them (`case 1: case 2: case 3:`) is the deliberate way to make several values share one block, and you will see that pattern in real code. But code sitting after a `case` with no `break` is almost always a bug.

The gotcha to name in an interview is that even `default` participates in fall-through — it is not magically isolated at the bottom, so a missing `break` above it lets it run on a value it never matched. The modern fix worth mentioning is **Java 14 arrow syntax** (`case 2 -> ...`): each arm is self-contained, can never fall through, and can return a value as an expression. For new code, prefer it; the fall-through question really only matters for older code you maintain.

sections.title: Classic Switch Execution — With and Without break
sections.content:
This diagram shows what happens when `day = 2` in a classic switch with no `break` statements versus one where each case has a `break`.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A(["switch on day=2"]) --> B{"case 1?"}
    B -- "no match" --> C{"case 2?"}
    C -- "match!" --> D["Execute case 2 body"]
    D --> E{"break here?"}
    E -- "NO (fall-through)" --> F["Execute case 3 body"]
    F --> G{"break here?"}
    G -- "NO (fall-through)" --> H["Execute default body"]
    H --> I(["End of switch"])
    E -- "YES" --> I
    G -- "YES" --> I
```

Without `break`, the matched case opens a gate and execution pours through every case below it. `break` closes the gate after each case.

sections.title: Switch Fall-Through at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Match|~Jumps to the case|execution starts here|no auto-stop|inherited from C
blue|No break|~Falls through|runs cases below|even default runs|the classic bug
emerald|break|~Stops the switch|only matching case runs|add to every case|unless grouping
rose|Arrow syntax|~Java 14+ fix|case V -> ...|no fall-through|case A, B -> groups

sections.title: The Bug: One Match, Three Lines Printed
The Fix: Arrow Syntax That Can't Fall Through
The One Time Fall-Through Is a Feature, Not a Bug
When Fall-Through Is Intentional
sections.content: Occasionally **intentional fall-through** groups multiple `case` values that share code — `case SATURDAY: case SUNDAY: ... break;`. That's legitimate. But code after a `case` without `break` is almost always a bug unless documented with `// fall through intentionally`. With Java 14+ arrow syntax you group cleanly: `case SATURDAY, SUNDAY -> "Weekend";`, which is clearer and removes the entire class of bugs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `break` in even one case** — the matched case and every case below it all execute, so you silently run extra logic and return wrong results from code that compiles without a single warning.
- **Treating classic `switch` like if-else** — if-else branches are mutually exclusive, but classic `switch` is sequential after a match, so reasoning about it as "only one branch runs" is the root cause of fall-through bugs.
- **Forgetting `default` falls through too** — it isn't magically isolated at the bottom; if the case above it has no `break`, `default` runs even when its value never matched.
- **Not knowing arrow `switch` exists** — sticking to classic `switch` in new code keeps the fall-through footgun around when Java 14+ `case V ->` removes it entirely.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Fall-through** — execution continues through later cases until `break` or end.
- **break** — the explicit stop that prevents fall-through.
- **Classic switch** — needs `break` in every case.
- **Intentional grouping** — stacking `case A: case B:` shares one block.
- **Arrow syntax** — Java 14+ `case V ->` never falls through.
- **default** — also participates in fall-through; it isn't isolated.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
This is a **code-reading trap**, so let me trace what actually happens. Say you `switch` on the value 2, with cases for 1, 2, 3, and a `default`. When `case` 2 matches, Java doesn't just run `case` 2 and stop — it jumps in at `case` 2 and then keeps executing straight down: `case` 3 runs, `default` runs, all of it, until it hits a `break` or the end of the block. So **one match prints three things**. That surprises people because they picture `switch` like if-else, where only the matching branch fires. Classic `switch` **isn't mutually exclusive** — the `case` labels are entry points, not gates, and that includes `default`, which falls through just the same.

That's why **every `case` needs a `break`**. The nuance worth raising is that fall-through is sometimes deliberate: if you stack `case` labels with no code between them — `case` Saturday, `case` Sunday sharing one block — that's a **legitimate grouping pattern**. But actual code after a `case` with no `break` is almost always a bug. My real recommendation is that for any new code I write, I use the **Java 14 arrow syntax**: case value, arrow, result. Each arm is self-contained, there's no way to fall through by accident, and it can return a value as an expression. The fall-through question really only matters now for maintaining older code.

speakable_v2.hook: Miss one `break` in a classic `switch`, and execution doesn't stop. It falls straight through every case below the match.

beats.text: Fall-through means a `switch` keeps running past the matching case when there's no `break`. It jumps in at the match, then runs every later case, until it hits a `break` or the block's end.

Java inherited this from C. It's handy on purpose, since stacking cases lets a few values share one block. But a forgotten `break` becomes a bug, so Java 14 added arrow syntax that never falls through.

items: With no `break`, a match at case two runs case two, then case three, then default. All of them.
With a `break` after each case, only the matched case runs.
Stacking labels with no code between them lets several values share one block, on purpose.

beats.text: Picture a `switch` on the value two, with no breaks. Case two matches, then control falls into case three and default. So one match prints three lines. Here's the non-obvious bit: default falls through too, so it runs on a value it never matched.

items: The sharp edge: forgetting one `break` silently runs extra cases and returns a wrong result.
In new code, prefer Java 14 arrow `switch`. Each arm's self-contained and can't fall through.

speakable_v2.cap: So add a `break` after each case, unless you're grouping on purpose. In new code, arrow switch kills the whole problem.
